plot_extraction.response_text:
Aboard a schooner sailing from Pensacola to Vera Cruz, passenger Samuel Warriner decides to celebrate Thanksgiving with a traditional plum pudding. He supplies the cook, Cornwallis Jones, with a recipe and brandy, but the pudding arrives decorated with rooster feathers instead of holly. When it is set alight, it erupts dangerously because Cornwallis has replaced the brandy with kerosene.

Suspecting that the cook drank the brandy, the captain and boatswain Prince frighten the superstitious Cornwallis by pretending that a nautical manual is a Bible prescribing drowning as the test and punishment for brandy thieves. Faced with being thrown overboard with a grindstone around his neck, Cornwallis confesses that he drank the liquor, blamed the devil for tempting him, and substituted kerosene so the pudding would still burn.

The crew laughs at his elaborate excuse. Warriner then conducts a mock funeral for the ruined pudding, solemnly throws it overboard, and marks its sinking with a blast from the foghorn before everyone returns to work.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written as a retrospective first-person sea yarn, narrated by a seasoned merchant sailor whose practical outlook, prejudices, limited education, and dry self-awareness shape the entire account. The narrator speaks as though addressing companions informally, using conversational pivots such as “But as I said,” direct appeals to the reader, incidental recollections, and personal judgments. This creates the impression of an anecdote told aloud rather than a polished literary memoir. His reliability is partial: he reports events clearly but casually reveals his own ignorance, vanity, racial prejudice, and susceptibility to shipboard folklore. Occasional moments of self-deprecation—particularly his admission that his history is “a bit uncertain”—make him both comic observer and participant.

The diction combines nautical vocabulary, nineteenth-century American colloquialism, and deliberately nonstandard grammar. Terms such as “mate,” “bo’s’un,” “watch and watch,” “all hands,” “beam ends,” “aft,” and “lee bulwarks” establish an occupationally specific maritime setting without extensive explanation. The narrator favors contractions, dropped endings, vernacular forms, and idioms such as “come to time,” “half heeled over,” and “parted our braces.” Exaggerated similes—swallowing lies “like an albacore does a flying-fish,” being knocked over “with a fish-hook,” or looking like “an oar with clothes on”—give the prose a salty, performative humor. Profanity is partly censored with dashes, suggesting periodical publication conventions while preserving the roughness of sailors’ speech.

Sentence structure is generally loose, cumulative, and speech-like. Long sentences gather qualifications, comic asides, and afterthoughts through coordinating conjunctions, while short exclamations and fragments sharpen moments of surprise: “Holy Moses!” or “Kerosene!” Parenthetical remarks mimic a storyteller leaning aside to explain a character or invite the audience into the joke. The narrative repeatedly delays its main action with character sketches and contextual digressions, but these apparent detours establish the social hierarchy aboard ship and prepare the later comedy. Punctuation is expressive and abundant, particularly dashes, exclamation marks, semicolons, and quotation marks, reinforcing the sense of animated oral delivery.

Dialogue dominates the central portion and supplies much of the characterization. Captain Pratt’s blunt profanity, Warriner’s ceremonious and pompous standard English, the narrator’s practical vernacular, and Prince’s and Cornwallis’s heavily represented dialect create sharply differentiated voices. Comic friction arises from collisions between registers: elevated rhetoric meets galley mishap, Biblical solemnity conceals improvised sailing directions, and Warriner’s mock funeral oration transforms a ruined pudding into a tragic hero. Repetition, malapropism, literal misunderstanding, and false erudition are recurring devices. Cornwallis’s claim to descend from Lord Cornwallis, his explanation that the devil forced him to drink the brandy, and Prince’s invented scriptural punishments all depend upon linguistic performance rather than subtle psychological narration.

The plot follows the compact architecture of a comic tall tale. An ordinary proposal—to make a Thanksgiving plum pudding—introduces an unfamiliar ritual and a volatile ingredient. Suspense builds through the cook’s boastfulness, the premature delivery of the brandy, and the substituted feathers. The pudding’s spectacular ignition provides the physical climax, after which the story shifts into a mock investigation. Prince’s counterfeit reading produces the confession, and Cornwallis’s elaborate excuse supplies a second verbal climax. Warriner’s theatrical burial of the pudding then functions as an extended comic coda, ending the episode with ritualized absurdity rather than moral punishment. Escalation is central: each attempt to repair or explain the original mistake makes the situation more extravagant.

The prevailing tone is boisterous, satirical, and affectionate toward shipboard disorder. Authority figures are repeatedly deflated: the captain is habitually drunk, the “Honorable” passenger is pompous, the narrator is poorly educated, and the cook survives through brazen invention. Even so, the story admires practical cleverness and theatrical wit, especially Prince’s manipulation of Cornwallis’s superstition and Warriner’s ability to turn disappointment into communal entertainment. Thanksgiving is treated less as a sacred observance than as a pretext for cultural collision, culinary farce, and temporary fellowship among mismatched people.

The piece also bears strong marks of the racialized popular humor of its period. Black characters’ speech is rendered through exaggerated eye dialect, and the narration repeatedly uses slurs, stereotypes, dehumanizing comparisons, and assumptions about ignorance, dishonesty, superstition, and racial sameness. These features are not incidental to the style; they are built into both characterization and comic mechanism. At the same time, Prince is portrayed as capable, literate, physically imposing, and strategically intelligent, while the white characters are also exposed as drunken, pompous, gullible, or ignorant. The result is a socially hierarchical ensemble comedy in which competence is distributed more broadly than the narrator’s prejudiced language initially suggests, though the representation remains firmly constrained by racist conventions.

Overall, the style blends maritime realism with tall-tale exaggeration, broad farce, dialect comedy, and mock-heroic rhetoric. Its signature movement is from plainspoken anecdote into increasingly theatrical absurdity, culminating in the grandiose elegy for the “dark and sodden mass.” The prose is most distinctive when low subject matter is expressed in elevated language, or when apparent solemnity masks deception. The intended effect is less refined irony than the communal pleasure of a vividly told, rhythmically paced, and extravagantly embellished shipboard story.

generation.response_text:
### THE BURIAL OF THE THANKSGIVING PUDDING

I have ate Thanksgiving dinners in places where a man had to hold his plate with one hand and fend off the furniture with the other; likewise I have gone without any dinner at all, unless you count three raw onions, a biscuit inhabited by more life than was wholesome, and a swallow of rain-water caught in an old boot. So I am not particular. A sailor that gets particular about his victuals had better ship as steward on a ferryboat, where the shore is always handy and the chickens do not have time to go bad between ports.

But the Thanksgiving I am going to tell you about was aboard the schooner *Ann Eliza*, bound from Pensacola to Vera Cruz with yellow-pine lumber, two crates of agricultural machinery that nobody could put together, and the Honorable Samuel T. Warriner as cabin passenger.

Why he was honorable I never rightly found out. Some said he had been in the Legislature of a Northern State, and some said he had merely been invited to run and had kept the title after declining. Cornwallis Jones, our cook, held that an honorable man was one who had fought a duel and killed both the other man and his second; but Cornwallis’s history was a bit uncertain. So is mine, for that matter, except where it concerns ropes, weather, wages, and the meanness of shipowners, which are four branches of human knowledge I have studied practical.

I was mate of the *Ann Eliza*. Captain Silas Pratt had command of her, if you could call it command when the Gulf was smooth. In bad weather the schooner commanded Pratt, and generally had him praying to three different denominations at once. He was a good navigator when sober, a fine seaman when half sober, and, when he was neither, he could still find the cabin bottle in total darkness with the ship half heeled over. He had a red beard, a temper like a wet cat in a flour barrel, and the habit of referring to every misfortune as an outrage specially directed against him by the United States Government.

Our bo’s’un was Prince Jackson—a long, square-built fellow, black as a stove-lid and twice as useful. Prince could read print, which gave him an advantage over half the forecastle and all of the afterguard except Warriner. He had once been in the navy, and had acquired there a solemn manner, a knowledge of regulations, and the ability to say “Very good, sir” in such a way that it sounded like “You’ll be sorry for this.” He could knot, splice, steer, rig a jury topmast, doctor a sprained wrist, and make a man ashamed of loafing without raising his voice.

Cornwallis Jones, on the other hand, could make coffee.

That is about as far as I care to go in praising him.

He called himself Cornwallis because, as he often explained, he was directly descended from Lord Cornwallis, who surrendered at Yorktown. How this descent had been managed was never made clear, and Prince said the only thing Cornwallis had inherited from his lordship was a genius for surrendering when surrounded. The cook was short and bow-legged, with a round face that always appeared to have just thought of something profitable. He wore a blue cotton shirt, checked trousers, and a white apron that had long since surrendered its original color to grease, soot, molasses, coffee, and the general drift of maritime cookery.

He was superstitious even for a cook. He believed in ghosts, signs, lucky bones, unlucky birds, the evil eye, drowned men knocking under the counter, and little invisible devils that lived in the flour barrel. If a knife fell point-first into the deck, he said company was coming. If it fell flat, he said bad weather was coming. If it stuck in his foot, he said the devil had thrown it; and once, when Prince asked whether the devil had also left the knife greasy, Cornwallis would not speak to him for two watches.

The *Ann Eliza* sailed out of Pensacola with a light northerly wind and every prospect of a decent passage. Warriner came aboard in a long black coat, a high collar, and a hat that looked too educated for the Gulf of Mexico. He was tall and spare, with whiskers alongside his jaw and a mouth made for public speaking. His baggage consisted of two trunks, six books, a silver-mounted cane, and a leather case containing papers that he guarded as if they were peace treaties.

He was going to Vera Cruz on business connected with railroads, land, mines, politics, or all four mixed together. Whenever anyone asked, he gave an answer about the inevitable development of continental resources; and by the time he had finished, the man that asked had forgotten the question.

He knew everything.

That was his chief weakness.

He knew navigation, though he had never been at sea; medicine, though he fainted when Simmons cut his thumb; agriculture, though he could not tell hay from tow; and the habits of foreign nations, though he called our Spanish phrase book a Portuguese dictionary. The first day out he informed Captain Pratt that a schooner ought not to roll so much.

“You don’t say!” says Pratt.

“It is due, I presume, to improper stowage.”

“No,” says Pratt. “It’s due to the sea being under her.”

Warriner considered this and said the captain’s explanation had superficial plausibility.

Now he was not a bad man. Pompous, yes; troublesome without meaning to be, certainly; but liberal with his tobacco, ready to laugh when the joke was not too plainly against him, and capable of giving a sailor half a dollar for carrying a trunk that the sailor had been ordered to carry anyhow. The crew got used to him, and he got used to us, though I do not believe he ever got used to Cornwallis’s cooking.

Nobody could.

The second morning Warriner lifted the cover off a dish, stared into it, and asked, “What is this?”

“Hash,” says Cornwallis.

“Of what?”

Cornwallis reflected. “Yesterday,” he says.

That answer bothered the Honorable Samuel for the rest of the day.

We made fair weather down the Gulf, keeping watch and watch, with the *Ann Eliza* walking along under all plain sail. The lumber was well stowed, the pumps sucked dry, and the only trouble was Captain Pratt’s conviction that the barometer was insulting him. We had been out about five days when Warriner came on deck after breakfast with one of his books tucked under his arm and a serious expression that meant he intended improving somebody.

“What date is Thursday?” he asks me.

“The twenty-ninth, by the log.”

“It is Thanksgiving Day.”

“Is it?” says I. “I thought Thanksgiving came according to where you happened to live.”

That was true in those days, or I thought it was. One governor would declare it one week and another governor the next, and a sailor outside soundings could miss three Thanksgivings and strike Christmas twice, according to the newspapers aboard.

Warriner said the day had been officially designated and was consecrated by custom.

“Well,” says I, “the weather may observe it, but I doubt the cook will.”

He gave me a reproachful look.

“Thanksgiving,” says he, “is not merely a date. It is an institution. It is the annual expression of a people’s gratitude for civil and religious liberty, domestic prosperity, agricultural abundance, and the beneficence of Providence.”

“Providence has not been liberal with the potatoes,” says I. “There’s half a sack left.”

He waved that aside. “Even at sea, among men temporarily withdrawn from the settled influences of home, the occasion should not pass wholly unnoticed.”

Just then Simmons, who was aloft greasing the foretopmast, dropped the swab, and it struck Warriner’s hat with a noise like a mud pie hitting a church door. That interfered with the settled influences of home for a minute or so; but after Simmons had apologized from above, Warriner picked up his hat, inspected the grease, and went aft to speak to the captain.

Pratt listened with one eye shut.

“Thanksgiving dinner?” says he. “All right. So long as it don’t cost me anything.”

“I propose,” says Warriner, “to provide the distinctive feature myself.”

“If it’s turkey, you’ll have to provide the turkey. The only live bird aboard is Cornwallis’s rooster, and he says that animal is descended from General Washington’s eagle.”

Cornwallis kept a lean red rooster in a slatted box beside the galley. He had bought it in Pensacola, meaning, so he said, to fatten it and sell it in Vera Cruz. As the rooster got less fat every day, we figured Cornwallis’s mercantile scheme was proceeding in reverse.

“No,” says Warriner. “A plum pudding.”

Captain Pratt opened the other eye.

“What kind of pudding?”

“A traditional English plum pudding—rich, substantial, and emblematic of the season.”

“I never knew a pudding that stood for anything except itself,” says Pratt. “But go ahead. If Jones can make it without blowing up the galley, he can make it.”

That last remark ought to have warned us.

Warriner went directly to Cornwallis, who was peeling onions with a knife in one hand and wiping his eyes with the other. I was near enough to hear, having business with a coffee cup.

“Jones,” says Warriner, “are you competent to prepare a plum pudding?”

Cornwallis drew himself up. “Mister Warriner, I is competent to prepare anything eatable, and some things that ain’t. I done cooked puddin’ for senators, governors, captains, colonels, bishops, and one genuine Egyptian prince.”

“Where was that?”

“Mobile.”

Warriner accepted Mobile as explaining the Egyptian prince.

“This must be a proper pudding,” says he. “Not a common boiled composition, but one made in the English manner.”

“I knows the English manner. My gran’father was English.”

“Your grandfather?” I says. “I thought he was Lord Cornwallis.”

“That’s the one,” says Cornwallis, not turning a hair. “He was powerful English.”

Warriner produced a folded paper. “Here is the recipe.”

Cornwallis took it upside down and studied it.

“Eggs,” says Warriner, “flour, breadcrumbs, suet, brown sugar, raisins, currants, citron, candied peel, nutmeg, cinnamon, cloves, and other ingredients specified there.”

“All present,” says Cornwallis.

“You haven’t got currants,” says I.

He looked injured. “Ain’t raisins currants when they small?”

“You have no citron either.”

“Citron is a manner of speaking.”

“Nor suet.”

At this he lost patience. “Mister Mate, if you aims to cook this puddin’, you better wear the apron. If I cooks it, then suet is what I says suet is.”

I left him to it. A cook’s galley is his castle, and a sensible mate does not attack a fortified position through the coffee steam.

Warriner had one more item. From beneath his coat he drew a squat bottle wrapped in brown paper.

“The final preparation is essential,” he says. “The pudding, when brought to table, is to be decorated with holly, saturated with brandy, and ignited.”

Cornwallis’s eyes fixed on the bottle. You could nearly hear them click.

“Ignited?” says he.

“Set on fire.”

“Yes, sir. I knows ignited. But why set good vittles afire after they cooked?”

“For the effect.”

Cornwallis looked doubtful. “Fire got a powerful effect on most things.”

“The spirit burns with a blue flame and imparts a delicate flavor. You will use only a portion in the pudding itself. The rest must be retained for the ceremonial serving.”

“Ceremonial,” says Cornwallis reverently.

He took the bottle.

I ought to mention that this transfer happened on Tuesday, two days before the dinner. Why Warriner trusted a quart of brandy to Cornwallis forty-eight hours ahead of its proper employment I cannot say. Some men can discuss continental resources by the hour and yet cannot see a cook’s hand reaching for a cork.

Prince saw it, though. He was coiling down a halliard just outside the galley.

“Better keep that bottle yourself, Mr. Warriner,” says he.

“My good man,” Warriner replies, “one must repose confidence in those charged with responsibility.”

Prince nodded. “Yes, sir. But you don’t have to repose the bottle with it.”

Warriner smiled in a forgiving way and told Cornwallis to guard it carefully.

“I guards it with my life,” says Cornwallis, clasping it to his apron.

“Guard it from yourself,” says Prince.

Cornwallis snorted and disappeared into the galley.

For the next two days he talked of nothing but that pudding. He hinted at secret ingredients. He chased Simmons away from the galley door with a ladle. He borrowed a canvas pudding bag from the steward’s stores, though what we had ever carried it for I do not know. He chopped, grated, pounded, mixed, sampled, and sang hymns in a voice like an anchor cable running through a rusty hawse-pipe.

At intervals there came smells from the galley—some pleasant, some doubtful, and one that drove the rooster into a fit of crowing.

On Wednesday afternoon Prince says to me, “That brandy’s gone.”

“Maybe some is.”

“All of it.”

“How do you know?”

“I’ve seen Cornwallis sober, and I’ve seen him with religion. Right now he’s got both together, which means he’s been drinking.”

I looked through the galley door. Cornwallis was leaning over a pot, singing that he was bound for the Promised Land, though judging by his steering he would not reach it on the first tack.

“Warriner will skin him,” says I.

“Mr. Warriner couldn’t skin a boiled onion,” says Prince. “But the captain might.”

Captain Pratt had already been making too free with his own bottle, so we did not report our suspicions. There is no benefit in telling one drinking man that another drinking man has drunk a third man’s drink. It only creates thirsty discussion.

Thanksgiving morning came in fine and clear, with a moderate breeze out of the northeast, long blue seas under us, and flying-fish scattering from the schooner’s bows like silver shavings. Warriner appeared in his black coat and clean collar. Captain Pratt shaved one side of his face, cut the other, and decided symmetry was not worth bleeding for. Prince had the decks washed down before eight bells, and even Cornwallis was quiet.

Too quiet, as I now remember.

Warriner had planned the dinner for two o’clock, so both watches might have some share in it. We were not to have turkey, but Cornwallis roasted a leg of pork and produced sweet potatoes, preserved apples, salt beef, pickles, biscuits, and a gravy that would have caulked a deck seam. The captain contributed two bottles of wine from his private locker after first holding them to the light and grieving over them. Warriner made a speech about gratitude. Simmons said amen in the wrong place. The schooner gave an easy roll, and a pickle slid off the table into Pratt’s lap.

Still, it was a good dinner.

The men of the watch below ate forward, but the pudding ceremony was to include all hands. Warriner insisted on it. He said a festival drew its significance from communal participation; and as Cornwallis had locked the galley after dinner, there was nothing else to participate in.

At last the cook appeared in the companionway carrying a great oval dish.

He had arranged the performance with more ceremony than a launch. He wore his cleanest apron, which looked dirty at a distance but clean near the bottom, and he held the dish high before him. Behind him came the cabin boy with a box of matches.

The pudding was black, round, and heavy-looking. It had the shape of a cannonball that had begun to melt. Something stuck out all around its crown in a ragged circle.

Warriner stared.

“What is that decoration?”

Cornwallis beamed. “Holly, sir.”

“That is not holly.”

“No, sir?”

“It is feathers!”

They were feathers, beyond dispute—red and yellow tail feathers from Cornwallis’s rooster, set upright around the pudding so it resembled an angry island chief or a Methodist hat after a hurricane.

“Holly has green leaves and red berries,” says Warriner.

“Ain’t none aboard.”

“Then why did you use feathers?”

“Feathers is festive.”

“Festive!”

“Yes, sir. Look at a peacock.”

Captain Pratt, who had already consumed his share of the wine and was reaching into future shares, said the feathers made no difference if the pudding was fit to eat.

Warriner shut his eyes for a moment, perhaps communing with domestic prosperity. Then he rallied.

“The garnish is irregular,” says he, “but the central tradition remains. Place the dish here, Jones.”

Cornwallis set it in the middle of the cabin table. The men crowded in the doorway and along the companion ladder. Prince stood aft with his arms folded. I noticed that he had stationed himself nearest the open skylight.

Warriner examined the pudding again.

“Has it been properly saturated?”

“Yes, sir,” says Cornwallis.

“With the brandy I gave you?”

There was the smallest pause.

“With the spirits provided, sir.”

Prince caught my eye.

Warriner took up a long spill of paper and lit it from the cabin lamp.

“Gentlemen,” he says, holding the little flame aloft, “we are separated by many leagues from our homes, but not from the associations that render home sacred. This pudding, humble though its surroundings may be—”

“Humph!” says Pratt, for the gravy had begun troubling him.

“—is an emblem of continuity. It links the wandering mariner with the domestic hearth, the present with the past, and appetite with gratitude.”

“Set her afire before she founders,” says Pratt.

Warriner touched the spill to the pudding.

Holy Moses!

That pudding did not burn with any delicate blue flame. It went off like the eruption of a volcano that had been saving up since Creation. There was a roar and a great yellow sheet of fire leaped to the cabin beams. The rooster feathers flashed, curled, and sailed blazing through the air. One landed in Pratt’s beard, another in the gravy, and a third went up the sleeve of the Honorable Samuel’s black coat.

All hands parted our braces at once.

I went over backward across the settee. Simmons tried to climb the companionway through two larger men and got wedged like a bung in a barrel. Captain Pratt slapped his beard, swore at the Government, and knocked the wine over. Warriner spun around beating his sleeve while the cabin boy threw a basin of water at him and hit the captain instead.

The pudding kept burning.

It burned like a tar barrel. Flames ran over it, under it, and around it. The dish cracked with a sound like a pistol shot. A river of blazing liquid crawled across the table toward the captain’s papers.

Prince moved then. He seized the folded tablecloth, flung it over the pudding, caught the whole smoking bundle in his hands, and pitched it onto the deck. I got a bucket from the scuttle-butt and poured water over it.

That made things worse for a second. The fire spread over the water in bright, greasy tongues.

“Kerosene!” shouts Prince.

“Kerosene!” says I.

“Kerosene?” says Warriner, whose dignity had been badly singed but not destroyed.

Prince smothered it with a second cloth, and this time the flames died, leaving the cabin full of black smoke and a smell fit to knock over a lighthouse with a fish-hook. We opened the skylight and companion doors. Men coughed, cursed, laughed, and stepped on each other. The rooster, suddenly deprived of most of his ornament, crowed from the galley as if the whole entertainment had been arranged in his honor.

Captain Pratt stood dripping beside the table, half his beard frizzled and a piece of raisin plastered to his forehead.

He looked at Cornwallis.

Cornwallis looked at the cabin boy.

The cabin boy looked at the pudding.

The pudding looked like h—ll with the fires out.

“What,” says Captain Pratt very softly, “did you pour on that thing?”

Cornwallis clasped his hands over his apron.

“Brandy, captain.”

Prince bent down, touched a finger to the wet deck, smelled it, and wiped his hand on Cornwallis’s apron.

“Kerosene,” says he.

There was a silence.

I have seen silences aboard ship that were calm and pleasant, and silences before a squall, and silences when the mate finds the man at the wheel has been steering by the wrong star. This silence was the kind that tells one party to begin running while he still owns legs.

Cornwallis did not run. There was nowhere to go but the foretop, and Prince could have pulled him down by looking at him.

Captain Pratt’s face went from red to purple.

“You infernal, lop-eared, galley-haunting son of a scorched frying-pan!” he says. “Did you try to burn my ship?”

“No, sir!”

“Did you soak that pudding in kerosene?”

Cornwallis swallowed.

“It got kerosene tendencies.”

“Tendencies!”

“Yes, sir. Some vittles naturally takes after lamp oil.”

Warriner stepped forward. His right cuff was burned away, his coat smelled like a refinery, and one whisker was shorter than the other, but he spoke as if addressing the Senate.

“Jones, I entrusted to you a bottle of high-quality French brandy.”

“You did, sir.”

“Where is it?”

“In the pudding.”

“The pudding contained kerosene.”

Cornwallis looked at the black remains with surprise. “Then that brandy must have altered powerful.”

Captain Pratt made a noise deep in his throat.

Prince leaned toward me and says quietly, “If the captain hits him now, we’ll never get the truth. Let me try him.”

“How?”

“There’s more than one way to sound a cook.”

Pratt had begun rolling up his sleeves.

“Captain,” says Prince, “before you discipline him, we’d better proceed according to maritime law.”

Pratt stopped. Captain Pratt had respect for maritime law whenever it promised to hurt somebody else.

“What law?”

“The law concerning theft of ardent spirits at sea.”

“There’s a law for it?”

Prince gave him his navy look. “Very strict law, sir.”

I knew Prince was inventing, because there is no sea law that deals with theft of liquor separately. If there were, no vessel could carry a full crew past Sandy Hook. But Pratt swallowed the statement like an albacore does a flying-fish.

“What’s the penalty?”

Prince glanced at Cornwallis, who had gone gray around the lips.

“We’ll have to consult the Scripture.”

“Scripture?” says Warriner.

“Old sea custom, sir. Captain keeps the ship’s Bible in his cabin.”

Pratt did not own a Bible, and Prince knew it. The nearest thing was Bowditch’s *American Practical Navigator*, a thick book with tables, rules, and enough figures to frighten any honest man.

Pratt understood the wink I gave him, though he took some time about it.

“Yes,” says he. “The Bible. Bring it out.”

I fetched Bowditch from the shelf and handed it to Prince. The cover was worn, the pages yellow, and it looked solemn enough to convict a bishop. Prince laid it on the table, first sweeping away a burnt feather and two currants.

Cornwallis watched him with his eyes bulging.

“Now,” says Prince, opening the book near the section on lunar distances, “this here offense falls under the Book of Nebuchadnezzar, chapter eight, ‘Concerning Cooks, Stewards, and Such Persons as Misappropriate Strong Waters.’”

Warriner coughed into his hand.

Captain Pratt bit his lower lip.

I turned toward the skylight, because if Cornwallis saw my face the trial was over.

Prince ran his finger down a column of logarithms.

“Here it is. ‘If any man, being cook aboard a vessel over ten tons burden and under three hundred, shall drink, conceal, embezzle, convert, swallow, sip, taste, or otherwise remove from lawful service any rum, brandy, gin, whisky, cordial, wine, shrub, or spirituous medicine entrusted to him for culinary purpose—’”

Cornwallis lifted one hand.

“Does it say brandy particular?”

“It says brandy in capital letters,” Prince replies.

“Oh, Lord!”

“‘—then shall that man be examined before the master, mate, bo’s’un, passenger, and such other witnesses as have not themselves drunk the evidence.’”

Captain Pratt cleared his throat and stepped a little farther from the wine bottles.

Prince continued: “‘And if the accused shall deny the offense, a grindstone shall be made fast about his neck with a new manila line, not less than three-inch circumference—’”

“New line?” I says, entering into it. “That’s wasteful.”

“Scripture is Scripture,” says Prince.

“Go on,” Pratt ordered.

“‘—and he shall be cast over the lee bulwarks in water exceeding six fathoms in depth. If innocent, he will float, the same being the sign appointed for innocence. If guilty, he will sink, the same being proof of guilt.’”

Cornwallis’s knees parted company.

“A man with a grindstone ain’t going to float!” he cried.

Prince frowned at him. “You disputing the Bible?”

“No, sir, but I knows grindstones.”

“Then you understand the seriousness.”

Warriner turned away abruptly and appeared interested in the barometer. Simmons made a choking sound at the companion door, and I kicked him on the shin.

Prince read on: “‘And after sinking, the offender shall remain below until three bells of the next watch, unless he sooner confesses.’”

“How he going to confess under water?” Cornwallis demanded.

“That,” says Prince, “is his lookout.”

Captain Pratt now entered into the spirit of it.

“Mate, what’s the depth here?”

“Thirty-eight fathoms by the last cast.”

“Plenty. Have a grindstone brought aft.”

We had a grindstone lashed near the foremast. It was not much of a grindstone, but Cornwallis had seen it often enough to know its weight.

“Simmons,” I called, “rouse it out.”

Simmons vanished with unnecessary enthusiasm.

Cornwallis looked from Prince to Pratt, from Pratt to Warriner, and from Warriner to me. He found no mercy, though he might have found several men close to bursting.

“Mister Prince,” he says, “read a little farther. Maybe there’s an amendment.”

Prince turned the page. “Amendment says two grindstones in case the accused has previously lied about his grandfather.”

Cornwallis clapped both hands to his head.

“That ain’t fair! A man’s family history is private!”

“Bring him up,” says Pratt.

At that moment Simmons and two others came aft rolling the grindstone along the deck. It bumped over the seams with a dreadful, judicial sound. They had already tied a length of rope through the center. Simmons, who could be quick when wickedness encouraged him, had even formed a noose at the other end.

Cornwallis backed against the cabin bulkhead.

“Captain,” says he, “I appeals.”

“To who?”

“The Government.”

“The Government has been after me for years,” says Pratt. “It won’t help you.”

“I appeals to Mister Warriner.”

Warriner turned, composing his face.

“The law must take its course.”

“I appeals to the rooster.”

The rooster crowed once from the galley.

“Unfavorable,” says Prince.

They rolled the grindstone nearer.

Cornwallis raised both hands.

“Hold on! I got a statement.”

Prince shut Bowditch but kept one finger marking the place. “Statement before or after immersion?”

“Before! Long before.”

“Proceed.”

Cornwallis drew a breath.

“That brandy was drank.”

“By who?” says Pratt.

Cornwallis looked upward.

“The devil.”

Nobody spoke.

“The devil,” he repeated, gaining confidence, “come into the galley Tuesday night, about two bells, and drank Mister Warriner’s brandy.”

Prince opened Bowditch again. “Devil ain’t listed as a member of the crew.”

“He was a visitor.”

“Did you invite him?”

“No, sir. Devil don’t need inviting. That’s his worst feature.”

“What did he look like?” Warriner asked, for he was beginning to enjoy the inquiry.

Cornwallis considered. “Short.”

“How short?”

“About my height.”

“Color?”

“It was dark.”

“How was he dressed?”

“In my shirt.”

Captain Pratt banged his fist on the table. “You drank it!”

“No, sir. The devil drank it through me.”

This distinction seemed important to Cornwallis.

He went on rapidly, with one eye on the grindstone.

“I had put that bottle behind the flour barrel, just where Mister Warriner told me to preserve it—which he never told me no such thing, but it was a natural place. Then I heard a voice say, ‘Cornwallis!’ I turns around, and ain’t nobody there. Voice says, ‘Cornwallis, take one little taste, because you don’t know if that brandy fit for the Honorable Samuel T. Warriner.’ I says, ‘Get behind me, Satan!’ Then the voice says, ‘I is behind you already, and the corkscrew is in the second drawer.’”

Prince’s shoulders began to shake, but his face stayed solemn.

“I took one little taste for safety,” Cornwallis continued. “It was fit. Then the devil says, ‘Maybe it ain’t fit all the way down the bottle.’ I says, ‘Away with you!’ He says, ‘Just one more.’ After that he put the bottle to my mouth.”

“With your hand?” I asks.

“He used the hand convenient.”

“Yours?”

“At that time he had possession of it.”

“How long did this possession continue?” Warriner inquired.

“Till the bottle was empty.”

“And then?”

“Then he departed.”

“Leaving you drunk,” says Pratt.

“Leaving me afflicted.”

Captain Pratt picked up the rope end.

“And the kerosene?”

Cornwallis’s expression became almost noble.

“That was where I tried to save Thanksgiving.”

“Save it!”

“Yes, sir. Wednesday morning I wakes up and finds the brandy gone by supernatural agency. I knows Mister Warriner expects the pudding to ignite. I knows all hands expects the blue flame. I says to myself, ‘Cornwallis, you has been visited by trouble, but you got responsibilities.’ There wasn’t no more brandy. Captain had his cabin locked.”

At this Pratt unconsciously felt for his key.

“So,” Cornwallis went on, “I studies what else burns. Pork grease burns, but smells common. Turpentine burns, but tastes sharp. Kerosene burns beautiful. I only used enough for ceremony.”

“You soaked it!” says Prince.

“The pudding was thirsty.”

“And you expected us to eat it?”

“After the fire burned the kerosene off.”

There it was. The complete case, confession, excuse, theology, and culinary principle all in one. I have heard lawyers take two days to make less sense.

For half a minute nobody moved. Then Simmons let out a squeak at the doorway. I started laughing. Prince dropped his head on Bowditch. Warriner’s solemn face cracked, and even Captain Pratt, with his burned beard and wet trousers, gave a roar that shook the cabin lamp.

All hands followed.

They laughed on deck, in the companionway, and forward by the windlass, though most of them had heard only pieces. A sailor does not need the whole joke if everybody else is laughing; he takes his bearings from the noise and comes in under full sail. Simmons sat down on the grindstone. The cabin boy leaned against the bulkhead and wept. Prince tried to read the punishment again, but got no farther than “three-inch circumference.”

Cornwallis watched us suspiciously.

“So there ain’t no such Scripture?” he says at last.

Prince held up Bowditch. “Every word printed right here.”

Cornwallis peered at the columns. He could recognize figures, if not much else.

“The Bible got an uncommon amount of arithmetic.”

“That’s the wages of sin,” says I.

His suspicion increased, but the danger had passed. Captain Pratt told him he was a condemned nuisance, docked him the price of the brandy, and ordered him to clean the cabin, scrape the pudding off the table, and never again attempt to save a holiday.

Warriner rescued what remained of his coat and contemplated the pudding.

It lay on the wet cloth, a dark, sodden, split mass, studded with half-burned raisins and giving off a thin smoke. One rooster feather still stood upright in the top. No man could have looked at it and thought of home, unless his home had lately burned down.

“I cannot permit it to end like this,” Warriner says.

Captain Pratt wiped his eyes. “You thinking of eating it?”

“Certainly not.”

“Then let it end.”

“No,” says Warriner. “It has played too memorable a part in our observance. It deserves formal disposition.”

He lifted the pudding, cloth and all, and carried it on deck.

“What now?” I asks.

“A burial at sea.”

That set the men laughing afresh, but Warriner remained grave. He ordered all hands aft, and Pratt—who would have agreed to a coronation by then—gave permission. Prince rigged a small board as a bier. The ruined pudding was laid upon it. Someone placed the scorched feather across the top. Cornwallis was made to stand at the head as chief mourner, though he said he had galley work.

The schooner moved steadily southward, her sails drawing pale against the afternoon sky. The sea was deep blue, with white caps here and there, and the sun laid a bright road westward. It was foolish, of course, but there are moments aboard ship when foolishness comes nearer to being necessary than sense. We had been away from shore, we had eaten too much, nearly burned the cabin, frightened a cook with a navigation book, and laughed until our ribs hurt. A ceremony was the natural next disaster.

Warriner stood beside the lee bulwarks. His black coat was scorched at the cuff, his collar had wilted, and there was soot across his cheek. Yet when he began speaking, he might have been dedicating a monument.

“Shipmates,” says he, “we are assembled to consign to the keeping of the deep the mortal remains of what was intended to be a plum pudding.”

Captain Pratt bowed his head. Prince nudged Simmons, who removed his cap.

“Conceived in generosity,” Warriner continued, “compounded in ignorance, decorated in misapprehension, and consumed by an element for which it possessed an unnatural affinity, it has completed a brief but extraordinary career.”

Cornwallis muttered that the recipe was bad to begin with.

“Silence in the mourners,” says Prince.

“It came among us,” says Warriner, “as a symbol of domestic fellowship. It leaves us as a warning against misplaced confidence, unauthorized substitution, and the indiscriminate use of petroleum.”

“That’s Scripture,” Pratt whispered.

“It united all ranks in expectation, separated them with remarkable speed at the moment of ignition, and reunited them in laughter. Though denied the honorable destiny of being eaten, it has not existed in vain.”

This was true. Few puddings have done more.

Warriner put one hand upon the board.

“Farewell, then, dark and sodden mass! Thou wert heavy in the dish, dangerous in the flame, and impossible in the mouth. No holly crowned thee, but the feather of a rooster whose confidence survives the loss. No delicate blue radiance attended thy final hour, but a conflagration visible, I have no doubt, to vessels beyond the horizon. The ocean receives thee. May no fish be injured.”

“Amen,” says Simmons.

The board was tilted.

The pudding hesitated at the edge, as if it had reconsidered Vera Cruz, then slid over the lee bulwarks and struck the water with a heavy splash. It floated for perhaps three seconds, black and round amid the foam. Then it turned once, showing the last red feather, and sank stern first—or pudding first, there being no stern to it.

Warriner raised his hand.

Prince had fetched the hand foghorn from its locker. At the signal he blew one long, mournful blast.

The note went out over the Gulf like a sick bull calling through a drainpipe.

At once the rooster answered from the galley.

That finished what dignity remained. All hands broke up laughing, Captain Pratt went below to dry his trousers, the watch returned to the braces, and Cornwallis hurried forward to see whether the devil had meddled with supper.

By sunset the cabin was scrubbed, though it smelled of kerosene for the rest of the passage. Warriner and Prince became good friends after that. The Honorable Samuel said Prince possessed a remarkable gift for forensic invention, and Prince replied that a navigation book was as useful as a Bible if the other fellow could not read either one.

As for Cornwallis, he never admitted that Bowditch was not Scripture. He only said some Bibles were written more nautical than others. He also claimed the pudding would have been excellent if we had let it burn another minute.

Perhaps it would.

I have eaten worse.

# The Lighthouse at the End of the Road

On the morning the sea disappeared, Mara Venn was repairing a clock.

It was a small brass carriage clock, no larger than her palm, and it had stopped at seventeen minutes past four. Its owner, Mrs. Pell, claimed this was the exact minute her husband had died, though Mara knew the clock had not worked for at least six months before that.

People preferred meaningful failures.

Mara sat behind the counter of her workshop with a lens pressed to her eye, coaxing a bent spring back into place, when the bells began ringing in the harbor.

Not the chapel bell. Not the market bell. These were the iron warning bells fixed along the seawall, each one pulled by a separate rope, each one producing the same blunt, panicked note.

She removed the lens and looked through the window.

Everyone in Bellweather was running downhill.

Mara placed the clock beneath a cloth, locked the workshop door, and followed.

Bellweather had been built on a slope of black stone, its houses stacked one above another as if seeking a better view. At the bottom lay the harbor, the breakwater, and the old road that ran east along the cliffs toward the lighthouse. Beyond them, until that morning, there had always been water.

Now there was none.

The sea had withdrawn beyond the horizon.

Fishing boats lay tilted in the mud. Anchors, broken masts, and pale ribs of forgotten ships emerged from the exposed seabed. Fish twisted in shallow pools. Farther out, where the sea floor became a gray plain, dark shapes stood like ruined towers.

The townspeople crowded the seawall in silence.

Old Noll, who had sailed for forty years, took off his cap.

“It’ll come back,” someone whispered.

“Course it will,” said another.

But no one sounded comforted.

Mara found her younger brother, Eli, standing on the wall itself, one hand shielding his eyes. He was nineteen, thin as a mast, with a dark curl of hair falling over his forehead.

“Get down,” she said.

He obeyed, though reluctantly.

“Do you see it?” he asked.

“See what?”

He pointed east.

At the end of the cliff road, three miles from town, the lighthouse stood against the white sky. Its lantern was burning.

It should not have been.

The lighthouse had been abandoned for eleven years, since the winter their father vanished.

Mara stared at the distant glow. It turned slowly behind the glass, pale in daylight.

Eli said, “Someone’s there.”

“No.”

“The lamp didn’t light itself.”

“Old machinery wakes sometimes.”

“Machinery doesn’t buy oil.”

She took his arm and pulled him away from the seawall. “We’re going home.”

“I’m going to the lighthouse.”

“You are not.”

He looked at her with the particular expression he had perfected at eight years old: injured defiance, sharpened by the certainty that she had wronged him merely by becoming his guardian.

“The sea goes missing,” he said, “and Father’s lamp starts burning. You don’t think that means something?”

“I think this town has had enough excitement for one morning.”

“You always think meaning is a mistake.”

“Usually it is.”

But even as she said it, she remembered their father’s coat hanging beside the kitchen stove, dripping rainwater onto the stones. She remembered his hand on the door latch and his voice saying, Stay with your brother. I’ll be back before dawn.

He had gone to the lighthouse during the worst storm in living memory. By sunrise the storm had broken, the lantern had gone dark, and their father was gone.

No body had ever been found.

For years Eli had asked questions. Mara had not. Questions were mechanisms: take them apart, and you often discovered there was nothing inside.

By noon, the mayor had ordered everyone away from the harbor. It made little difference. People gathered on rooftops, in upper windows, and along the eastern road. Some prayed. Some packed carts. Others ventured onto the seabed to collect stranded fish and objects revealed by the vanished water.

The exposed world smelled of salt, weeds, and ancient rot.

Mara returned to her workshop, but she could not concentrate. Every clock seemed too loud. They ticked from the shelves in uneven chorus, filling the room with hundreds of tiny footsteps.

At seventeen minutes past four, Mrs. Pell’s carriage clock began to run.

Mara had not finished repairing it.

She watched the hands move.

From somewhere far below the floor came a deep sound, too low to be thunder. The windows trembled. All the clocks stopped at once.

Then someone pounded on the door.

Mara opened it to find a barefoot girl from the baker’s house.

“It’s Eli,” the girl gasped. “He took the east road.”

The sky had turned yellow by the time Mara reached the edge of town. She carried a lantern, a coil of rope, and their father’s old compass, though its needle had pointed east instead of north since the night he disappeared.

The cliff road was narrow and patched with grass. On one side rose dark hills; on the other, the land dropped toward the empty seabed.

Eli’s footprints marked the dust.

Mara walked quickly.

Below her, townspeople wandered among the remains of shipwrecks, appearing tiny as beetles. They had found cargo scattered in the mud: green bottles, coins worn smooth, ceramic jars sealed with wax. Their shouts drifted upward.

The farther Mara went, the quieter the world became.

She passed the first milepost, then the second. The lighthouse grew taller ahead of her. Its white paint had peeled away, exposing the stone beneath, yet the lantern revolved steadily.

The old keeper’s cottage crouched beside it.

At the gate, she found Eli’s coat caught on a nail.

“Eli!”

No answer.

The lighthouse door stood open.

Inside, the circular room smelled of dust and hot metal. Rusted tools hung from hooks. A table leaned against the wall. The spiral staircase rose around a central column and vanished into darkness.

Mara lit her lantern.

“Eli?”

A footstep sounded above.

She began to climb.

The stairs remembered the sea. Their iron rails were crusted with salt, and each step groaned like a ship’s hull. Halfway up, she noticed a line of fresh oil running down the central column.

At the top, she pushed through a trapdoor into the lantern room.

The great lens turned around a flame so white it hurt to look at. Gears moved beneath the floor, polished and bright despite years of neglect.

Eli stood by the window.

Beside him was their father.

Mara dropped the lantern.

It struck the floor but did not break.

Silas Venn looked almost exactly as he had eleven years earlier. His beard was still black, his shoulders still broad beneath his weather-stained coat. Only his eyes were different. They seemed faded, as though he had spent too long staring into a distance no one else could see.

“Mara,” he said.

She could not breathe.

Eli’s face was wet with tears, but he was smiling.

“He came back,” he said.

Mara gripped the iron railing. Beneath shock, beneath the impossible recognition, anger rose with such force that it steadied her.

“You left us.”

Silas lowered his head. “I did.”

“For eleven years.”

“For you.”

She laughed once, without humor. “Don’t.”

“The light had to be kept.”

“The light was dark.”

“Not here.”

He looked toward the vanished sea.

Outside, evening had begun to gather. The exposed seabed extended farther than sight, cracked and gleaming. The sun hung low over it like a red coin.

Silas placed his hand against the turning lens.

“That storm eleven years ago wasn’t a storm,” he said. “Not entirely. Something came close to our shore. Something that lives beneath distance, where maps run out.”

Eli listened as if hearing scripture.

Mara said, “You expect me to believe that?”

“No. I expect you to look.”

He pointed through the eastern glass.

At first Mara saw only the empty plain. Then the beam swept across it, and shapes appeared in the light.

There were thousands of them.

Tall, narrow figures stood across the seabed, motionless and black. Some were miles away; others waited near the base of the cliffs. They had no faces that Mara could see, only smooth heads bent toward the lighthouse.

When the beam passed, they vanished.

Mara stepped back.

“What are they?”

“Travelers,” Silas said. “Or hunters. I never learned which.”

“And the sea?”

“A door. A wall. Maybe both. It retreats once every hundred years, and they cross while the way is open. The light keeps them from climbing.”

Eli wiped his eyes. “Where have you been?”

“In the lamp.”

Mara stared at him.

Silas smiled sadly. “Not my body. My time.”

He showed them the mechanism beneath the lens. It resembled no lighthouse machinery Mara had ever seen. Rings of brass revolved inside one another without touching. At their center hung a glass vessel filled with white fire.

“Someone must wind it,” he said. “But winding the light costs time. A minute for a turn. An hour for every circuit of the beam.”

Mara thought of the past eleven years, of growing from eighteen to twenty-nine while her father remained unchanged.

“You gave it your time,” she said.

“The sea returned before it took all of me. I thought the lamp would sleep until the next opening.”

“But it didn’t,” Eli said.

“No. The door has opened early.”

Another low tremor passed through the tower.

Far below, the black figures shifted.

“How long until the sea comes back?” Mara asked.

Silas looked at the clock mounted above the lens. It had only one hand, which crept across a blank face.

“By dawn, perhaps.”

“And the lamp?”

“The mechanism is failing. I’ve held it since sunrise, but the spring is nearly gone.”

For the first time, Mara noticed that his right hand was locked around a brass lever. The skin of his fingers had turned gray.

She moved closer. The mechanism clicked irregularly.

A clock, she thought. However strange its purpose, however terrible its price, it was still a clock.

“Let me see.”

Silas hesitated.

“Let her,” Eli said. “She can fix anything.”

“Not anything,” Mara replied.

But Silas released the lever.

The moment he did, he aged.

Black hair whitened. His back curved. Lines spread across his face as if drawn by an invisible pen. In seconds he became the old man he should have been.

Eli caught him before he fell.

The lens slowed.

Outside, the figures began moving toward the cliff.

Mara knelt beside the mechanism. There were familiar parts—escapement, spring, gears—but their arrangement was wrong. The machine did not measure seconds. It devoured them.

A fractured tooth on the main wheel caught at each rotation. The spring had warped. Worse, the glass vessel was dimming.

“Can you repair it?” Silas asked weakly.

“Yes,” Mara said.

She was not sure.

From below came the sound of metal scraping stone.

Eli helped their father sit against the wall, then joined Mara. “Tell me what to do.”

“Take the small wrench from my bag. No, the smaller one.”

The tower shuddered.

Through the window, Mara saw the first black figure reach the cliff road. It moved without bending its legs. Behind it came another, and another.

She removed the damaged wheel. The mechanism resisted, pulling at her hands with a sensation like cold water. As she worked, memories flashed before her—not images recalled, but moments removed.

Her mother singing while washing dishes.

The taste of an apple stolen from the market.

Eli’s first word.

Each vanished as quickly as it came, leaving an absence she could feel but not name.

She jerked her hand away.

“It takes time from anyone who touches it,” Silas said. “Not only the keeper.”

“You might have mentioned that.”

“I wanted you to leave.”

The beam stopped.

Darkness rushed against the glass.

Something struck the tower door below.

Eli seized the lever and pulled.

The lens lurched into motion. He cried out.

A streak of white appeared in his hair.

“Let go!” Mara shouted.

“No!”

“You don’t know what it’s taking.”

“Neither do you.”

Another strike shook dust from the ceiling.

Mara examined the broken wheel. Mrs. Pell’s carriage clock flashed into her mind: the brass, the size, the repaired spring. The clock sat beneath a cloth in her workshop three miles away.

But the compass was in her pocket.

She took it out. The needle still pointed east, trembling toward the fire.

Its case was brass.

Its inner wheel was almost the right size.

Almost.

She forced the compass open with the wrench. The needle spun wildly once freed. She removed the gear beneath it, filed two teeth, and fitted it into the lighthouse mechanism.

It caught, slipped, then turned.

“Now the spring,” she said.

There was no replacement.

Below, the tower door splintered.

Silas struggled upright. “There’s another way.”

Mara already understood.

The spring could be wound by hand. A person could power the light directly, trading life for motion.

“How much?” she asked.

“Until dawn?”

“Yes.”

“All that remains.”

Eli’s hands tightened on the lever.

“I’ll do it,” he said.

“No,” Mara and Silas said together.

Eli looked from one to the other. “You both got to decide everything. Father decided to leave. You decided never to talk about him. You decided I was a child forever. I’m deciding now.”

“You’re deciding to die,” Mara said.

“I’m deciding Bellweather doesn’t.”

A crack appeared in one of the lower windows. A long black hand curled through it.

The turning beam swept over the hand, and it recoiled, smoking.

Silas crawled toward the mechanism.

“I began this,” he said. “Let me finish.”

“You’ve already paid,” Mara told him.

“So have you.”

“Not enough.”

There it was: the arithmetic she had carried for eleven years. She had resented Silas for leaving, resented Eli for needing her, resented the clocks for continuing when her own life had narrowed into work, meals, bills, and locked doors. She had believed herself robbed of youth, and now the machine offered a way to spend what remained.

Meaningful failures.

Meaningful sacrifices.

Perhaps people preferred them because ordinary pain was harder to bear.

Mara studied the mechanism again.

A clock did not create time. It divided motion.

“Father,” she said, “you told me the lamp takes an hour for every circuit.”

“Yes.”

“From the keeper.”

“Yes.”

“Why only one keeper?”

Silas frowned.

Mara looked down toward Bellweather. Lamps shone in windows across the hillside. Hundreds of people waited there, watching the lighthouse.

“One spring breaks under too much force,” she said. “So you distribute the load.”

She took the rope from her shoulder and tied it to the winding lever.

“Mara,” Eli said, beginning to understand.

“Run it down the stairs. Through the door, if you can. Then take it to town.”

“The things are on the road.”

“The light will cover you each time it turns.”

“What happens between turns?”

“Run faster.”

Eli grinned despite himself. He looped the rope around his arm and opened the trapdoor.

Silas tried to rise.

“You stay,” Mara said. “Tell me when to pull.”

Eli descended.

For several terrible minutes, Mara heard nothing except impacts below and the irregular grind of the gears. She held the lever, surrendering seconds one by one. Her hands wrinkled. A year passed through her like a fever. Then two.

The rope tightened.

Far down the road, a figure ran west carrying its end.

The beam turned. Black shapes recoiled from Eli’s path.

He reached the first houses after sunset.

Mara could not see what happened there, but the rope began to move. Slowly at first, then steadily.

The lever pulled itself.

The lens brightened.

Across Bellweather, people emerged from their homes. They took hold of the rope: fishermen, bakers, children, widows, shopkeepers, thieves, and councilmen. More lines were tied to the first. They stretched through streets and around posts until the whole town was linked to the lighthouse.

“Pull!” someone shouted.

The cry traveled uphill, voice by voice.

The light blazed.

It took a little from each of them.

A gray hair. A forgotten afternoon. A day not yet lived. The cost spread among hundreds became small enough to bear.

The black travelers climbed the cliff in silence, but the beam drove them back. All night the people of Bellweather pulled together while Mara guided the repaired gears and Eli ran between town and tower carrying messages.

Near midnight, rain began falling upward from the seabed.

By two, pools gathered across the empty plain.

At four seventeen, every clock in Bellweather started ringing.

The sea returned not as a wave, but as a reflection. Water unfolded across the world from horizon to shore, covering wrecks, mud, and black figures. For one instant the travelers stood beneath the clear surface, their smooth faces turned toward the light.

Then the depths swallowed them.

The lighthouse flame went out.

Dawn rose over a calm sea.

Silas Venn died with his children beside him.

They buried him on the hill above Bellweather, where he could see both the town and the lighthouse. Nearly everyone attended, though some could not remember exactly why they wept.

In the weeks that followed, people discovered what the night had cost them. The mayor had lost the memory of his wedding breakfast. Mrs. Pell had lost three months from the end of her life, which she claimed she had not intended to use anyway. Old Noll woke with white eyebrows. The baker’s barefoot daughter forgot how to whistle and had to learn again.

Mara had lost seven years.

Her hair was streaked with silver, and fine lines marked the corners of her eyes. Eli apologized whenever he looked at her until she threatened to throw him into the harbor.

Together they reopened the lighthouse.

They replaced the broken stairs, cleaned the lens, and ran new ropes from the winding mechanism to a wheel in the town square. Every household agreed to take a turn, one minute each year, so the lamp would never again depend on a single keeper.

As for Mrs. Pell’s carriage clock, Mara returned it fully repaired.

“It still stops at seventeen past four,” Mrs. Pell complained the next day.

“Then perhaps it means something,” Mara said.

Mrs. Pell regarded her suspiciously, unable to tell whether she was joking.

Years later, travelers passing through Bellweather often remarked upon its clocks. They were everywhere: above doors, in gardens, on the harbor wall, and even carved into the mileposts along the eastern road. None showed quite the same hour.

The townspeople did not mind.

They had learned that time was not one thing. It was a spring under tension, a road taken in darkness, a rope passed from hand to hand.

And every evening, as the lighthouse beam crossed the water, Mara paused at the window of her workshop and watched it return.

Again.

Again.

Again.
